But the play is like a mosaic in which the glittering individual pieces obscure the big picture.
The writing is shrewd and impassioned but it lacks bite.
Yazji's play, doggedly heartfelt as it is, also tugs in too many different directions.
Goats has the potential to be a fascinating and illuminating piece but too often it’s clunky and confusing.
The play, translated by Katharine Halls, is too long and trying to do too much at once.
Too much of the storytelling isn’t all that clear and the piece is often under-dramatic, as Yazji sets about debunking the martyrdom myth we were always expecting to be debunked.
The serious subject-matter is diminished by an overlong running-time, underpowered scenes and disjointed dialogue.
A study in martyrdom and in keeping going when lives are upended, Liwaa Yazji's play devolves into shouty overkill in the second act.
There is no question that Goats is a moving and powerful play in this production directed by Hamish Pirie.

As a piece of informative theatre however, it is neither particularly surprising, revelatory or especially entertaining (even allowing for the unpredictable and sometimes comedic contribution of the four-legged stars).
There’s something seriously wrong with a production when the most present, captivating performances come from livestock.
Goats, Royal Court review - unfocused and muddled
Because while the goats are endlessly watchable, the play really is not.
Even if the macabre absurdity of hoping to substitute goats for lost children is a strong indictment of government policy, Goats is slack, humourless and boring.

cn.t: Critics find this Syrian war play well-intentioned but dramatically inert, with the six live goats on stage proving far more captivating than the human drama—a distraction that undermines the serious subject matter.
